title: Continuity of care and carer
blurb: Explain what continuity of carer is, what the current evidence shows, and how national policy now targets it safely.
question: Jade, 19, lives in one of the most deprived areas of the city. Her trust runs a small midwifery continuity team but staffing is stretched. Why might Jade be offered this model, and what does the evidence say it achieves?

teach.h: Care that joins up, carer she knows
teach.body: Formally, continuity of care means care that is consistent and coordinated across services and settings; continuity of carer means care from the same midwife or a small team across pregnancy, birth and the postnatal period (SPM 2.4, 2.5). In plain English: continuity of care is a joined-up journey; continuity of carer is a familiar face on that journey, who already knows her story.
teach.cite: NMC Standards of proficiency for midwives 2.4, 2.5

rows.label: Focus
values: A relationship with a known midwife

rows.label: Who provides
values: Named midwife in a small team

items.label: Better Births: a midwife in a team of 4 to 6 for every woman
NHS England letter: no national target date
Three-year plan: roll out only with safe staffing
Prioritise Black, Asian, minority ethnic and most deprived

teach.body: The National Maternity Review set out that every woman should have a midwife who is part of a small team of 4 to 6 midwives, based in the community, who knows the woman and family and provides continuity through pregnancy, birth and postnatally. Each team should have an identified obstetrician, and the midwife should liaise closely with obstetric, neonatal and other services so care is joined up.

teach.h: Cochrane review 2024: continuity vs other models
head: Outcome
Other models
Midwife continuity
Certainty
teach.caption: Sandall et al., Cochrane 2024: 17 studies, 18,533 women. Women also reported a more positive experience.

teach.text: Older sources (Better Births and the 2016 Cochrane review) said continuity reduces preterm birth. The 2024 update found little or no difference in preterm birth, with low-certainty evidence. Key the current finding: more spontaneous births, fewer caesareans and instrumental births, a better experience.

root.label: Can the trust staff MCoC safely?

teach.caption: No national target date: local plans that fit local staffing, focused on women who benefit most.

teach.body: Jade, 19, is booked with a continuity team of six midwives, and Aisha becomes her named midwife, giving most of her antenatal care with a direct phone line (CG110 1.4.4). The team's identified obstetrician reviews her raised blood pressure without Jade losing her known midwife. Jade is offered this model because the trust prioritises young women and those in the most deprived areas, where continuity is most likely to make a difference.

items: Continuity of care is joined-up systems; continuity of carer is a known midwife or small team.
Better Births: team of 4 to 6, community based, with an identified obstetrician.
Cochrane 2024: more spontaneous vaginal births, fewer caesareans and instrumental births, better experience; little or no difference in preterm birth.
Since 21 September 2022 there is no national target; MCoC continues only with safe staffing.
Priority: women from Black, Asian and minority ethnic groups and the most deprived areas.

summary: You can now distinguish continuity of care from continuity of carer, describe the Better Births model and summarise the current evidence accurately. You can also explain why national targets were removed and which women are prioritised.

A.q: In the Better Births (2016) model, how many midwives should make up the small community team that provides continuity for each woman?
options: 4 to 6
2 to 3
8 to 10
A.why: Better Births recommended every woman has a midwife who is part of a small team of 4 to 6 midwives based in the community.

whyNot.1: Teams of 2 to 3 are smaller than the Better Births model.
whyNot.2: 8 to 10 is larger than the recommended team.
whyNot.3: 10 to 12 would dilute the relationship that continuity depends on.

A.q: What did NHS England's letter of 21 September 2022 change about midwifery continuity of carer?
options: It set March 2023 as the target for full rollout
It withdrew continuity from midwifery education
It limited continuity to women with complex needs
It removed the national target date for MCoC
A.why: The letter said there would no longer be a target date for MCoC; local services develop plans that work for them, subject to safe staffing.

whyNot.0: The letter removed target dates rather than setting a new one.
whyNot.1: Students are still to be taught the MCoC model, as the NMC confirmed.
whyNot.2: The letter asked for a focus on vulnerable groups, not a restriction to complex needs.

A.q: According to the 2024 Cochrane review, which outcome is more likely for women receiving midwife continuity of care models?
options: Caesarean birth
Induction of labour
Spontaneous vaginal birth
Postpartum haemorrhage
A.why: Midwife continuity likely increases spontaneous vaginal birth (66% to 70%, moderate certainty).

whyNot.0: Caesarean birth is likely reduced, not increased.
whyNot.1: There may be little or no difference in induction of labour.
whyNot.3: There is likely little to no difference in postpartum haemorrhage.

B.q: A trust can staff only a few continuity teams. According to NHS England policy, which women should be prioritised for them?
options: Women expecting their first baby in the area
Women planning to give birth at home
Women from minority ethnic groups and deprived areas
Women aged 35 or over at the booking visit
B.why: Core20PLUS5 names continuity of care for women from Black, Asian and minority ethnic communities and the most deprived groups as its maternity focus.

whyNot.0: Parity is not the national basis for prioritising MCoC.
whyNot.1: Planned place of birth is not the prioritisation criterion.
whyNot.3: Age is a mortality risk factor, but the stated priority is ethnicity and deprivation.

B.q: Which arrangement best describes continuity of carer rather than continuity of care?
options: Electronic records shared between hospital and GP
A written handover when she moves between units
A standard care pathway used by every team
One small team caring for her from booking to postnatal
B.why: Continuity of carer is about the relationship: the same midwife or small team across pregnancy, birth and the postnatal period.

whyNot.0: Shared records support continuity of care, the joined-up system.
whyNot.1: Handover supports continuity of care between settings.
whyNot.2: A common pathway is about consistency of care, not a known carer.

B.q: A trust cannot meet safe minimum staffing even for its existing continuity teams. What did NHS England's September 2022 letter say it should do?
options: Suspend MCoC and transfer women safely to other pathways
Keep current teams and expand to one new area this year
Keep current teams and await a national target date
Book new women into MCoC and reduce postnatal visits
B.why: Trusts unable to meet safe minimum staffing for existing provision should immediately suspend it and ensure women are safely transferred to alternative pathways, considering their individual needs.

whyNot.1: Expansion requires staffing to meet minimums for further rollout.
whyNot.2: Existing provision must be suspended when it cannot be staffed safely.
whyNot.3: Booking more women into an unsafe model increases risk.

C.q: A student midwife says, 'Continuity of carer is proven to cut preterm birth.' Which response reflects the 2024 Cochrane review?
options: Yes, high-quality evidence shows a reduction of about 24%
No, low-certainty evidence suggests little or no difference
No, continuity models are linked with more preterm births
Yes, but the reduction is seen in twin pregnancies
C.why: The 2024 update found there may be little or no difference in preterm birth (6% in both groups; low-certainty evidence). The earlier 2016 review reported a reduction.

whyNot.0: That reflects the superseded 2016 review, not the 2024 update.
whyNot.2: The review found no increase in preterm birth.
whyNot.3: The review did not report a twin-specific benefit.

C.q: Jade, 17, books at 11 weeks. She is anxious about attending a busy hospital clinic. Which plan best follows NICE guidance for young women?
options: Refer her to obstetric-led care because of her age
Book the standard schedule with the next free midwife
Offer a named midwife who provides most of her care
Arrange all visits in the hospital for scan access
C.why: CG110 1.4.4: offer women under 20 a named midwife who takes responsibility for and provides most of their antenatal care, with a direct-line number.

whyNot.0: Age under 20 alone is not an indication for obstetric-led care.
whyNot.1: Rotating staff loses the continuity NICE recommends for this group.
whyNot.3: CG110 1.4.1 favours age-appropriate community care, not hospital-based care.

C.q: In the Better Births model, what medical support should each team of continuity midwives have?
options: A neonatologist attached to every team
A GP who carries out all antenatal checks
A consultant who leads every woman's care
An identified obstetrician who can advise
C.why: Better Births: each team of midwives should have an identified obstetrician who can get to know the service and advise as appropriate.

whyNot.0: Better Births did not attach a neonatologist to each team.
whyNot.1: Antenatal checks are provided by the midwifery team, not a GP.
whyNot.2: Women at low risk remain under midwife-led care; the obstetrician advises.

reteach.title: A familiar face, when it is safe
reteach.question: Why is continuity of carer valued, and why did the national target go?

blocks.body: When a woman knows her midwife, she is more likely to have a spontaneous vaginal birth and a positive experience, and less likely to have a caesarean or instrumental birth. But the model needs enough midwives. In 2022, with workforce pressures, NHS England removed the national target date and told trusts to run MCoC only where staffing is safe, prioritising the women who benefit most.

blocks.text: Do not quote the old preterm-birth benefit. The 2024 Cochrane review found little or no difference in preterm birth.

explain.body: SPM 2.4 asks midwives to work across settings to promote continuity of care and carer. SPM 2.5 asks them to provide continuity of midwifery carer across the whole continuum, for women with and without complications.

test.q: SPM 2.5 expects midwives to provide continuity of midwifery carer for which women?
options: Women with no identified risk factors
Women with and without complications
Women planning to give birth at home
Women having their first baby
test.why: SPM 2.5 covers the whole continuum of care for women and newborn infants with and without complications and additional care needs.

whyNot.0: The standard is not limited to women at low risk.
whyNot.2: Continuity applies whatever the planned place of birth.
whyNot.3: Parity does not limit the standard.

explain.body: A personalised care plan for every woman; a midwife in a community team of 4 to 6 who knows her and her family; an identified obstetrician per team; close liaison with obstetric and neonatal services.

test.q: According to Better Births, where should continuity teams of midwives be based?
options: In the obstetric unit
In the neonatal unit
In GP practices
In the community
test.why: Better Births described small teams based in the community who know the woman and her family.

whyNot.0: Teams are community based, working closely with the obstetric unit.
whyNot.1: Neonatal units are a specialist service, not the base for continuity teams.
whyNot.2: GP practices are not the base described in Better Births.

explain.body: Cochrane 2024 (17 studies, 18,533 women): midwife continuity likely increases spontaneous vaginal birth and reduces caesarean and instrumental birth, may reduce episiotomy, and improves experience. Preterm birth: little or no difference. Effects on fetal loss and neonatal death are very uncertain.

test.q: What did the 2024 Cochrane review conclude about continuity models and caesarean birth?
options: They likely reduce caesareans
They likely increase caesareans
They have no effect on caesareans
They double caesarean rates
test.why: Midwife continuity likely reduces caesarean birth from 16% to 15% (moderate certainty).

whyNot.1: The direction of effect was a reduction.
whyNot.2: A small reduction was found with moderate certainty.

explain.body: 21 September 2022: no national target date. Trusts with safe staffing continue; those safe for existing teams only stop rollout; those unsafe even for existing teams suspend and transfer women safely. The 2023 three-year plan and Core20PLUS5 focus continuity on minority ethnic and the most deprived women.

test.q: Why did the 2023 three-year delivery plan ask trusts to consider MCoC rollout in line with NHS England's September 2022 principles?
options: To ensure safe staffing first
To end continuity models
To set new local targets
To limit it to home births
test.why: The plan links any MCoC rollout to the September 2022 principles on safe staffing.

whyNot.1: The plan kept continuity as a goal, focused on those who benefit most.
whyNot.2: The 2022 principles removed targets rather than adding them.
whyNot.3: Continuity is not tied to place of birth.
